text: David knew what sheep were like.
They needed a shepherd. They needed food, water, safety, and someone watching when they didn't know danger was near.
So when David thought about Yahweh, he used the picture he knew best.
Yahweh was his Shepherd.

A good shepherd didn't merely own sheep. He stayed with them. He led them to grass when they were hungry and to quiet water when they needed rest. He knew when they were tired, frightened, or wandering toward trouble.
David had done that work with real sheep.
Now he saw that Yahweh had done it for him. God had guided him, guarded him, and restored his soul when life had worn him down.
David could say, "I shall not want," because he wasn't alone in the field. He belonged to the Shepherd who knew the way.
That was enough for the day.
The sheep didn't have to know every path. They had to know the shepherd's voice.
David had learned that too. He didn't always know what was ahead, but he knew who was leading him.
The Shepherd was good, and the Shepherd was near.
The path didn't stay on green hills.
Sometimes it went down into shadow. David called it the valley of the shadow of death, and he knew what those words meant.
Danger could be real. Fear could be close.
But Yahweh was closer.

A shepherd didn't abandon the sheep when the path turned dark. That was when his presence mattered most. The valley wasn't a sign that the shepherd had failed. It was part of the journey he would lead them through.
David didn't say there was no danger. He said he would fear no evil because Yahweh was with him.
The comfort wasn't that the valley was easy. The comfort was that he didn't walk it alone.
The rod and staff were in the Shepherd's hands. One could strike the enemy. One could guide the sheep back to the path. David knew what both meant.
Protection and correction. Both were mercy.
The valley had shadows, but shadows weren't the final word.
David kept walking because the Shepherd was there. Fear could speak, but it didn't get to lead.
Yahweh led.
That was why David could pass through the valley and not make his home there. He was going through.
Then the picture changed.
David was no longer only a sheep in the field. He was a guest at a table, and Yahweh Himself had prepared it.
The enemies were still there, but they weren't in charge.
The table was.
A table means welcome. It means someone has made room for you. It means provision isn't thrown at you from a distance, but placed before you with care.
David said Yahweh prepared a table before him in the presence of his enemies. That didn't mean the enemies had disappeared. It meant they didn't control the meal.
God did.
The cup was full. The oil was poured. Honor replaced shame, and fear didn't get the seat at the head of the table.
David could sit because Yahweh had invited him. The enemy could watch, but the enemy couldn't cancel the Shepherd's care.
The table was a quiet kind of victory.
Not loud. Not rushed. Not anxious.
David didn't have to prove he belonged there. Yahweh had placed him there.
The cup overflowed because the Shepherd was generous.
More than enough. That was the sound of grace.
Psalm 23 ends with home.
David looked ahead and saw goodness and mercy following him all the days of his life. Not just one day. Not just the easy days.
All the days.
The Shepherd wouldn't stop being faithful.

Goodness and mercy didn't merely visit David. They followed him. That is a strong picture, like Yahweh's kindness staying close behind him through every road, every field, every valley, and every battle.
David's life had not been easy. He had known danger, sin, grief, enemies, and loss. Still, when he looked at the whole road, he could see that Yahweh had been faithful to him again and again.
The Shepherd had led him to grass. The Shepherd had walked him through shadow. The Shepherd had set the table. The Shepherd would bring him home.
David's confidence wasn't in his own strength. It was in Yahweh's steady care.
David wanted to dwell in the house of Yahweh forever.
That was the end of the song, and it was the deepest comfort. The sheep wasn't wandering forever. The guest wasn't leaving the table forever.
The Shepherd was bringing him home.
Yahweh had been with him. Yahweh would be with him.
Forever.
